review_text_raw:
This is not an easy game nor a polished one. I sense the direction of this game was focused towards a giant sandbox of snooping and somewhere along its devcycle someone said, "Hey, this isn't a game." Then someone else said, “Okay, we have all these things the player can do. Read emails, check contacts. Put people on watchlists… How do we make this into a game?” 

The answer of course was to have the player click on links, clicking on the right ones giving  the player points, or if they got it wrong taking points away. But that was too simple, and not very fun, so they added a couple tools to click on the links in different ways and it made it better. And the Devs (who by this point knew exactly how to use each different link clicking tools) said, “Behold! Fun!” And that’s probably as far as playtesting ever got; to the point where the small team of developers had fun playing their own game. 

This is always a problem with small indies with big visions,  they didn’t have time to playtest and get substantitive player feedback. And the biggest problem this game actually has is that the player doesn't receive feedback until  they’ve already failed. Of course, you can review these mistakes after you've failed, but with all the data you need to take in, it is difficult to parse exactly what you did wrong or even how you failed in some cases.

Despite these problems,  this game has there is a good core gameplay loop and a pretty fascinating story. KtK is a competent game in many senses and does not deserved to be tossed aside as a bad game when it is simly missing satisfying feedback.

With time I imagine this game’s player feedback will be fixed. And if it ever is, I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone with an interest in "connect the dots" style gameplay and Snowden Era cyberspying.  Right now, the only people I would recommend it to are people who not only love the genre and click on the right thing mechanics, but also have a high tolerance for failing and vigorously studying their failures and don't mind reading forum posts to figure stuff out.

Edit for patches: The developers have accomplished a lot in making the early gameplay more intelligible.

review_text_raw:
In a nutshell: A good game, with some great ideas, that needs some polish on the execution, with a number of technical and interface issues that drag down a good story and a great idea.

Put simply, the idea of a game where you move through the hierarchy of a sinister spying agency is a great one, and this game's greatest success so far in my time with it has been not only showing how quickly the power to snoop on everything and everyone can go wrong, but also, and crucially, how it can still also be a force for good. The story is I think the strongest point of the game for me, because it's depiction of the ironically named 'Department of Liberty' is not really as some cartoon villain 'Illuminati conspiracy' but as a government organisation set up in response to a great crisis which, at least initially, is comprised largely of ordinary people. Sure, some of the people you meet in the game are dubiously motivated at best, but the game reinforces in the narrative consistently that there are good people in the DoL, who genuinely believe the spying they engage in is justified and indeed, there are examples in game where the power you use does make a real difference.

I can't say much more without spoiling the hell out of the game, but suffice it to say, if story is what you want, the game offers an intriguing story, and while it may not be a Tom Clancy tale, I've found it engaging and compelling.

Likewise, the gameplay offers good challenge, requiring you to carefully dissect the data you sift through, looking not just for keywords early on but as time goes on, looking for more complicated and easily missed details, like tracing suspicious bank activity with logs of suspicious contacts, and working out if they match up or are a red herring. These shifting challenges do a reasonably good job of building on each other, with each clearance level you go through iterating on previous challenges with an extra layer of complexity, and this organic growth of difficulty is largely well-executed. But it does lead into the big problem in the game: communication.

This game has a real problem communicating with the player, and I think it's largely down to an interface that can be clunky and unintuitive. Partially this is down to bugs, like notifications on your phone not displaying so you're left staring blankly waiting for something to happen, to more egregious errors like typos in the keywords you're looking for, and contextual menus being hard to close once opened and obscuring the screen. These are all fixable issues thankfully, and while irritating, they don't for me drag the game down too much, but the sooner they are resolved, the better, and they are likely to irritate some players too much to continue.

Also, the game can be ambiguous in what the objectives of each day actually require. For instance, you might be asked to look for keywords, but the game isn't good at indicating whether you need a literal, case-sensitive match of the word, or a contextual match. For instance, if the keyword was 'Bomb Kit' and you saw a log that said 'making my own bombs in a kit', you might well flag that as suspicious, and logically, it totally is, but because the game is looking for a case-sensitive, exact match, it marks you down as wrong for it. Again, these issues are not exactly common, but they're infrequent enough to annoy, and for me are the biggest issue of all in the game, but again, can be fixed by the devs.

So in the end, I recommend this game, but I do it with an advisory: if you want a good story, with fun challenges and an engaging concept of government intelligence and the morality of that, then I highly recommend it, but make sure you go in right now knowing there are currently technical and design issues, and while these will likely be fixed, as of the time of this review they exist, and they can annoy. Hopefully you'll be like me, and able to see through the roughness to the diamond within, and enjoy the experience for what it is, not what you necessarily would like it to be.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What is this game?[/h1]
It is the foremost NSA-watch-the-world-from-an-office simulator you will find as of the time of writing this review, and possibly for a long time.

You play a young man, joining a government agency. The rabbithole goes deep, and you are thrusted into a position of Orwellian surveillance, intrigue and thrill.

Starting at the bottom, you analyze simple things. Metadata, browser history and try to piece together a puzzle that is very clearly Need To Know. Given only slight glimpses of what is truly going on in this world. As you progress, you will advance in rank, getting a higher and higher level of clearance, and quickly find yourself face to face with the choice of whether or not to use your access for the good of the agency, the government, the country. the people or even yourself. 

Utilizing your powers of cyber-espionage to predict and even outright uncover your flings interests and hobbies, getting the IRS to get off your back, finding your sister/brother during an emergency or even getting out of paying your rent.

It very quickly becomes apparent what kind of power it actually is you are trusted with, and you will immediately realize why exactly it is so dangerous if left unchecked.

Don't just take it from me. Take it from the very person who knows this the best when he retweeted the game
[i]"Art imitates life."
~Edward Snowden[/i]

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The graphic artstyle of this game is great. It's minimalistic, but still detailed in the way it is done. The whole layout gives a sense of a point-and-click adventure, and for all intents and purposes it is.

Graphically, this game is unique in the way it focuses on the mechanics and uses the art direction to enhance them. You're never distracted by what's on the screen or in your peripheral vision, yet even after many hours (I'm writing this after a 24 hour bender on this game) it never ceases to be interesting or captivating. Artistically, it's very clear it was drawn by somebody who is passionate about the game, and it shows.

[h1]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h1]
The game had a very rough start at launch, with virtually no tutorial. That has been corrected. The team behind this game are very active both on the games own Subreddit, taking into account all the reports being thrown at them and have now rolled out the fourth daily patch in a row. Where else do you see that?

The gameplay itself is good. However, I will be the first to admit that it can be un-intuitive. They have and still are taking steps to improve on this, but the game itself doesn't suffer that heavily under the previous or current issues. It plays like one would very much expect of a game of this type, yet it manages to do [i]so much[/i] with the established fundamentals of the game. Despite having pre-ordered this the moment I saw it almost half a year ago (it has been in development since 2016 and undergone many redesigns), I was honestly afraid that it would end up like most games of this caliber do, where you end up feeling the developers grasping at straws, and the game for its breath as it tries to reskin the same old mechanics and play them off as changes to the gameplay. The gameplay [b]does not change[/b], and thats strangely enough the charm and appeal.

Connect the dots as you chain together events from mere fragments of information such as e-mails, texts, social media, phone calls, browser history, bank account transcripts and decide the fate of the very people you've been spying on from behind your screen. Will you label them a threat for speaking their mind in, what they assumed to be total privacy and confidence, or will you stand up and become a whistleblower and help bring down this omniscient, omnipotent government entity?

You do unlock new abilities progressively as you pass through the ranks of this fictional quasi-NSA government agency, but they do not change the way the game plays, only improve and enhance upon it. All too often do you see games desperately trying to change its own formula throughout the span of the game, and it more often than not ends up sweeping the rug out from under themselves. You won't find that here.

I have never been much for point-and-click games. So much so that I own none except for Orwell and Need to Know. If you have played Orwell, you will without a doubt find yourself enamored with this title.

On a final note, I'll add that there is a story. Getting into it here wouldn't do it justice, and I haven't even completed the game yet. But it will draw you in. Seemingly unrelated events tie together into something larger, and as you scale the ranks of this clandestine government, denying counter-surveillance groups information (or perhaps supplying it yourself), so does the plot thicken and grow.

I would most definitely recommend this game to pretty much anybody who likes a captivating experience.

It is not without flaws, but the developers have rolled out daily fixes since release, and are obviously very passionate about this game. It's not early access, but it isn't a triple-A polished and buffed product, either. But it is getting there.

review_text_raw:
I like the premise and gameplay of this game, but so far - after 16 hours - the story advancement has been miniscule. And judging by the progress in "clearance levels" I'm in like half of the game. And it's pretty unrewarding and just really, really long. The core gameplay loop is pretty nice when you get different mission types or advancements in the story, but when you spread it over so many hours it becomes boring anyway.

I also believe there is an issue with difficulty, since there's no option to change it, and for the first like 4 or more clearance levels it is ridiculously easy (with one very hard mission thrown in every once in a while). But there's really no punishment for failure in story sense - you can absolutely botch an "investigation" (when you are for example looking for a suspect in waves and accidentally mark them as non-suspect in the first wave) and still succeed. Which makes sense from gameplay sense, but it's pretty immersion breaking, especially when you are still awarded with catching the criminal and such.

And coming from there - a lot of stuff in the game feels very forced. Like your "romance" / "date" or whatever just eventually appears in your apartment with no option to reject them. Sometimes you are presented with "options", but when you choose certain dialogues the game just ends (sometimes as if you almost won, and sometimes you just end up in jail and such) but in the end you always have to go back and choose the options the game wants you to.

And speaking of "going back" - there are no save slots; The game saves randomly and you can't go back. If you fuck something up because there was no tutorial or the description was misleading or you didn't get the gist of what you are looking for - tough luck, the game punishes you for that and you have to keep going forward. This issue is especially apparent with some mission types or evidence gathering that's poorly explained. One time I got everything wrong for misreading what the game wanted me to do (matching years of consecutive growth when something happens vs. matching just the last year of consecutive growth *with the thing that happened*). And there is more where that comes from.

I also encountered some minor visual bugs and UI annoyances. One of the bigger one is that "helpers" (people who you don't use your powers on and only help match evidence and such) are marked the same color on the map as the suspects. Well, some times. From the tutorial I think they are meant to be teal, but they're white like everyone else... Unless they are red for some reason, but only every once in a while (even in a single mission) before they are white again.

All in all I'm pretty conflicted in whether to recommend this game - [b]if you really like the core gameplay loop (go watch some videos) then sure, go for it[/b]. The annoyances are minor enough to really affect that too much. But [b]if you are like me, spending 16 hours to get into what is presumably half of the game with very repetitive gameplay and just tiny bits of story... You are better spending your time elsewhere[/b]. Just for comparison: I finished the whole playthrough of Prey 2017 in like 22 hours, and by the time I was at hour 16 I had discovered almost all of the story, everything about the station and Typhon, etc.

review_text_raw:
EDIT: I changed from not recommended to recommended. Because the game (tactics) change after reaching clearance level 8. Still the below criticizm is applied, but for a game with this pricetag it doesn't to that bad.

So i was hyped for this game from the start & a early kickstarter funder, but it feels like a disappointment for now.
I specially played this game for a few hours to see if it just has a slow start. But sadly it doesn't only have a slow start.. It keeps slow (might even call it boring). 
Only positive note i have at this moment is, that the story is well written and has some noticable real life scenarios.

Another bad thing (in my opinion) is the time it takes to unlock new ablilities. This only happens when you reach a new/higer clearence level. 
I have more then 4 hours into the game. And i only just unlocked clearance level 8 and therby new abilities. This takes to long in my opinion..

The game has the "beta" feel all over itself. Feels cluncky, UI is horrible to work with & windows get blocked constantly. Rules window should be movable at least.
Crashes at weird moments and nothings happening at the same point after restarting the game.

Also the evidence that needs to be collected, can be very conflicting. The rules states that something needs to be collected. But it it isn't directly linked to your suspect but a contact. The game states that you made a wrong choice.

Just as many i was hoping for a "Papers, Please" like gameplay and challenge, but than in a intelligence styled jacket.
This game is disappointing on all fonts:
- Gets boring soon, game also needs some kind of speed mode.
- Sometimes very unclear/conflicting what kind of evidence needs to be collected.
- You get new ways to check on people but no new tools to use, but only whit new clearance levels.
- Just point and click/memory playstyle. I miss some sort of typing involved (for example keyboard shortcuts), playing as an analist.
- Some times theres logic in "linking" people or suspects together early on. You just/simply can't... This is only possible when the game tells you to.
- (to hide spoilers) You do the same thing anywere.
- Buying stuff.. Ehh, whats the use of this? Whats the use of making money in this game anyway. I don't even have to pay rent.. 
- Weird saving structure. Log out before "End Session" aaaand start all over again with the same mission.
- When you "start over" a session by quitting the game. The location and names of the suspects is the same every time & also their logs.
- Crashes mid game (had three in less than 4 hours of gameplay).

It's just constantly doing the same thing.. Over and over.
This is the thing with most games and isn't that big of an issue. 

The issue with this game is, that there isn't enough variation in "what" to do. 
There is just to little to do to keep it interesting. It's way too late in the game & taking way too long to get there, if you even get there you're interest in this game is most likely already gone.

Still putting all the negative points aside. For their first (major) game, it's actually quite good.
I'm certain they will improve the game and crush some bugs in the oncoming days. So lets see how this plays out!

And i only just unlocked clearance level 8 and therby new abilities. This takes to long in my opinion.. The game has the "beta" feel all over itself. Feels cluncky, UI is horrible to work with & windows get blocked constantly. Rules window should be movable at least. Crashes at weird moments and nothings happening at the same point after restarting the game. Also the evidence that needs to be collected, can be very conflicting. The rules states that something needs to be collected. But it it isn't directly linked to your suspect but a contact. The game states that you made a wrong choice. Just as many i was hoping for a "Papers, Please" like gameplay and challenge, but than in a intelligence styled jacket. This game is disappointing on all fonts: - Gets boring soon, game also needs some kind of speed mode. - Sometimes very unclear/conflicting what kind of evidence needs to be collected. - You get new ways to check on people but no new tools to use, but only whit new clearance levels. - Just point and click/memory playstyle. I miss some sort of typing involved (for example keyboard shortcuts), playing as an analist. - Some times theres logic in "linking" people or suspects together early on. You just/simply can't... This is only possible when the game tells you to. - (to hide spoilers) You do the same thing anywere. - Buying stuff.. Ehh, whats the use of this? Whats the use of making money in this game anyway. I don't even have to pay rent.. - Weird saving structure. Log out before "End Session" aaaand start all over again with the same mission. - When you "start over" a session by quitting the game. The location and names of the suspects is the same every time & also their logs. - Crashes mid game (had three in less than 4 hours of gameplay). It's just constantly doing the same thing.. Over and over. This is the thing with most games and isn't that big of an issue. The issue with this game is, that there isn't enough variation in "what" to do. There is just to little to do to keep it interesting. It's way too late in the game & taking way too long to get there, if you even get there you're interest in this game is most likely already gone. Still putting all the negative points aside. For their first (major) game, it's actually quite good. I'm certain they will improve the game and crush some bugs in the oncoming days. So lets see how this plays out!

I'm gonna change my review to positive, because I can see the devs care for their game and they are  fixing the issues. The game still has flaws, but it's heading in the right direction.
Currently I'm CL 8, here are my fidings.
- As I see until now there is no punishment for making bad decisions, unless you kinda miss all the clues, where it can go game over. The only downside so far is to get less salary, still you can't do anything effective with the money you make other then decorating your house, or paying off the rent or helping your family.
- On the other hand I was sitting on 100% compliance for a couple of days, and i didn't get any benefit from it. Initially i thought you move through the levels according to your performance, but unfortunately it's all scripted. I understand it would be difficult, still a nice change if the devs could implement this.
- There is no pressure, no engagement. The time stops at 5pm and waits until you finish all the suspects, no matter how slow you are.
-There is no real weight of your decisions, as everything seems scripted. You get updates after each mission, what happens with the profile of the suspects. Still it's so irrelevant, probably you won't even remember what was in their profiles, and even if they appear ingame later, you won't remember that you've already seen them. (Or it might be only me) Maybe would be nice to implement a summary of DoL record for the suspects, stating your findings and the actions taken. 
-Mission 3 was a so called speedrun, still it doesn't seem any different than the other days.
-The whole game is really slow paced, feels sluggish. CL 10 and 9 is way too long for the amount of diverse actions you can do. It feels much like a grind.
- As a lot of others, I don't like the UI either. I think there are too many irrelevent staff on screen while you are in mission (Phone, ID, building, office), they all take space from the important infos, i struggle to have all the data and the rules for the mission on screen. Also I hate that the map is moving, it just gives an extra level of frustration, that i need to drag the map between profiles.
Sorry devs, I need to compare it to Papers, please. Need to know has a much wider scale, potential and story, still PP has much  more flavor, and there you can really feel the weight of your decisions.

Good game for mature children and teens, but most adults will be disappointed. The main game mechanic is "finding a needle in a haystack". Unfortunately, the haystack is tiny, and the needles are not very well hidden. You are provided a list of keywords to find in tiny documents, given basic criteria. The biggest challenge is making sure it is spelled correctly before highlighting it. I expected the game to be more investigatory, being able to follow leads, etc... this is not that kind of game.

Your character is a young adult, fresh out of college, working his/her first job. The story and the style of the dialogue was written to appeal to children. At one point, my friend in the game texts me to ask who was my high school crush. I immediately assume he is phishing for the answer to my security question to hack my password, but no. I'm overthinking. The game just does this to determine if your crush was a male or female, so it can introduce a new character into the game.

The icing on the cake for why I have to give this game a thumbs down... An anti-government group tries to extort me. There is no option to report this to the Department. I choose not to provide them any documents, because I take national security seriously, and then I lose the game. ---You must leak classified documents, or it is game over.

So much for Monomyth Games' "will you stand up for privacy, or help create an unstoppable police state?" ---Well, I'm forced to leak classified documents to terrorists, so I guess I don't have much choice in the matter.

Monomyth Games also writes, "You can also resist ... by aiding underground groups ... Or, you can just use all of that juicy classified information for your own personal gain. Your call." ---But it's not my call, because if you don't leak the classified information, it is game over.

The pitch made about the game misrepresents the actual game. I would have paid twice as much for the game if it delivered on what was promised, but as it is, I feel duped. They did a really good job on the graphics and interface design... moral dilemmas in stories are awesome, but you can't propose a moral dilemma to the player and then force a game over state if they choose to follow federal law.

Overall, a really cool game for the price.  A good bit of superficial bugs for something officially released since Oct 2018.  I am very happy to have backed it 3 years ago.

Okay, so here we go. I've reached up to CL 3 now and have played the alpha version of this game as well. It's quite a bit of fun and I'm enjoying it.  PLEASE TRY THIS GAME. THE GRIND PAYS OFF.

Pros:
Neat concept, reasonably well executed by what I understand is a fairly novice indy team.
Developers are fixing the bugs
The art style is neat  (was kind of getting tired of Indy game meaning pixelart)
The CODEX facts are kinda funny sometimes and the little easteregg info bits are a nice touch.
The story is reasonably engaging
Fun sort of puzzle-type game
Doesn't feel like papers please
Hope to see new stuff get added in future as Devs are being fairly responsive to community input
The UI is well-optimized (especially when compared to the Beta)
Soundtrack isn't bad either.
The characters do actually feel like real people.
Cons

Sometimes the rules aren't always super clear and this can lead to some serious mission screwups (however, fret not, even if you get a huge compliance ding you can either A) exit the mission before going home (this will restart it from the login screen or B) Just eat the compliance hit because usually the next mission is more forgiving it's usually a couple easy missions then a kind of tough one and then a few easier ones)

The missions can feel a little grind-y. 

There's some stuff missing that seems like it should be there (There's no stock trading system as promised, the shop only has a handfull of items to buy, no cars or anything like what was in the original trailer for this game).

The first couple CLs are a grind. I've got almost 17 hours into the game and I'm at CL 3 (you start at 10). The real fun doesn't really start until about CL 6 or so and I think that's pushing a couple people away from the game.

The Data selling thing is just kind of super annoying and stretches the gameplay out unnecessarily while adding little to the story.

Wish there were more character customization options. 


TL;DR: Neat indy game, responsive development team. Can be a little grind-y through the first bit but gets pretty good after that.

I really wanted to like this game. I saw Jon from MATN on Youtube try it and it looked liked my kind of thing. While I really like the premise, how it looks and some of the missions, unfortunately the experience has been frustrating. Mostly small things, but many small things which add up to an overall frustrating experience.

My general frustrations have been:
- Cluttered screen, especially when using a laptop when the screen is smaller.
- Evidence not demonstrating what the rules require but marked as missed when not chosen. (E.g. Evidence of someone telling a suspect to buy shares, when the rule says suspect must have bought shares. These are not the same thing, but the game considers them to be.)
- Moving background makes selecting the small dots difficult and no option to turn the movement off.
- You can choose incorrect evidence yet the immediate feedback says something which suggests it was in fact correct.
- Some rules weren't fully explained either in tutorial or in Peepr so got confused especially in the beginning.
- No way to re-evaluate a suspect once you've made a decision even if the day hasn't ended.
- No way to replay a day or restart unless you log out.
- Strongbox missions are sometimes very long winded and so get fed up quickly as the strongbox only seems to allow as much evidence as you can fit on the screen without scrolling. When on a 13inch macbook it fills up too quickly.

I think this game has a lot of promise, but it needs working on before I will consider recommending it.

Really awesome RPG/sim that has a great level of detail and involvement with the world. The quality writing and soundtrack combined with good formula make this a fun and immersive game. The gameplay maintains a good pace and overall found the UI to be very good along with helpful tutorials and tips. The element of challenge isn't too hard to be able to rise up as an agent, yet also requires a bit of concentration and practise to be able to reach max clearance levels.

I'm impressed with the way that this game brings together old school RPG elements like good writing and progression, along with nostaglic af animations and design - with great art and attention to details (like being able to see your own computer on screen as you 'work' during office hours). Ultimately the great production quality and gameplay creates a modern version of the RPG/sim that brings together many old and new elements

I have not finished the game!! This is one of the BEST dystopian simulations i've played. Similar to Orwell, as other reviewers have pointed out, but EVEN BETTER! 

Things I loved:
I love the challenge. It's definitely a game you have to pay attention to and make correct choices. 
There are different facets to the game that allows you to balance home and work life and develop numerous relationships. These are not optional. NPCs will just force you to talk through the phone or at work. 
Relevant story that builds onto itself and you are ultimately working towards the final goal which is to identify and locate Cloud Dweller ( i believe thats his alias) 
I like the characters. I like the story. It's very well written and done. And I love that I can be sassy with that dude at work that everyone hates. LOL 
It's a long and complex game. It was longer and has more content than I expected.
The dating app KILLS ME! Those profiles XD no wonder people are single.

Things I hated:
Some choices lead directly into game over. I ended the game multiple times unintentionally with no warning through dialogue selection. Like I was talking to the reporter/boyfriend/friend? Not sure of his purpose yet. Anyway, I accidentally said I worked at DoL and BAM! game over. Thankfully the autosave system allows you to log back in and pick up before you make that choice. But it was just so sudden and happened multiple times during different scenarios.
Everyone forces you to work for them. You have to keep selling secrets to keep your reputation up with everyone so they don't either blackmail you or fire you. It's annoying. I would rather have more choices. I don't like being two-faced and this game forces you to be that.

Overall - I still recommend it. I keep wanting to finish it and it has held my interest which few games do. However, I doubt I'll replay it. Either way - it's definitely worth the price! Buy it on sale if you can, but even $15 is still decent for this game.

KEEP UP THE GOOD WORK!

Writing this on release + 3 : it took a hot minute to get used to the UI which, as almost all other reviews mention, has a confusing flow and unintuitive button areas. After that, it's a great game. Strong comparisons to be made with Orwell of course, but so far I think I prefer Need To Know. There's buckets more narrative and the actual process of doing things is less of just a steps puzzle and more involved and interesting.

I was an early bird kickstarter backer and I've been waiting for Need To Know for a good long while. After a few hours of light play, I'm happy with the game so far. A little polish on the UX in the form of better interaction cues and guides and it'll go from fun with a rocky start to an excellent experience.

Alright where do i start. The surveillance concept is very interesting, and the realism of the whole thing made it deeply disturbing for me, which is a good thing, since it kept me on the edge of my seat many times. Gathering evidence can get tricky, there are many traps left and right, but the difficulty is fair. The UI could be better, especially in later clearance levels, where the evidence can get overwhelming. I love the art style though. The story is pretty good, although its tainted by the obvious illusion of choice.


However there are some things that i dislike very much, not because they are bad themselves, but because how the game interacts with or based on it. For instance, the game saves twice a day(ingame time) and creates a gazillion save points, which would be okay, if it were possible to load any other save point beside the last.


Very mild spoilers regarding game design:

Then, you can buy stuff, this got me excited, but it actually has 0 impact on anything aside your bank account, which again, has 0 impact on anything besides the possibility to buy stuff. So its basically a closed system of uselessness. The suspicion points are only used to 5 at max i think, the other 3 seem to be decoration until the very end game, and even then they dont affect anything either.

Spoiler End

Facit &tl;dr
Its a good game, has some flaws, but nothing major. Interesting setting, worth full price, any sale would be a steal.
If you like stuff like Orwell, papers please, beholder, you probably will like this, too.

review_text_raw:
I loved this game. Recommend.

Selling point:
The morally ambigious writing and the logical characters. The game makes you feel you are part of a 90s political thriller, set in the modern world.

Pros:
- writing is amazing
- puzzles are logical and set in the real world
- aesthetics are minimalistic, but cool (my only gripe is that some people looked bizarre),
- game duration (game changes pace once it gets slightly repetitive, which was welcome)
- world-building (despite its conspiracy context, the game is very much grounded in the real world both in terms of politics and technology, and everything felt contemporary, even in its future years)
- achievements (100% completion is based on completing the game, not on some wild goose chase)

Cons:
- UI (common visual glitches, although I do play on linux which may add glitches; animations are slow, changing suspects is slow, link puzzles between multiple suspects are slow not due to complexity of puzzle but due to UI problems; clicking on suspects is difficult even if you remove map scrolling)
- some puzzle solutions have obtuse or small consequences, could have kept its linearity but with some more impact on world, you do get some comics balloons for some optional objectives
- game does push you to become a government bot, even if your character disagrees wildly with that (but this is somewhat necessary from a writing standpoint).

In Brief:
This is a very good game for someone who is interested in mass surveillance, abuse of power, corporate capitalism, world politics, solving puzzles, and in general feeling like a special part of an important conspiracy.

Has a fair bit of length and an intriguing story to start. I feel the ending was slightly telegraphed and predictable and the Balancing of Seb, Renege, and Denys was all too easy as there was almost always 3 pieces of data to sell to each. For me at least the time limit was never an issue so I never felt that "crunch factor" that the clock instills in the player. While playing though do prepare to be paranoid in future online activities and disgusted with your in game actions. All in all a good game for those looking for an intriguing narrative.
